%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the

\begin{abstract}
Reducing energy consumption is a primary goal for the mobile telecommunication industry, with strong environmental and economic sustainability implications. The main target for savings is the Radio Access Network (RAN), which is responsible for 73\% of the total energy costs incurred by operators.
The go-to strategy here is reducing the number of active RAN carriers at locations and times where the demand is reduced and can be served with a smaller wireless capacity.
While the scientific community has been proposing a plethora of complex solutions to switch-off underutilized carriers, production networks largely rely nowadays on static threshold-based strategies that run at individual RAN equipment and are thus very simple to deploy.
However, there are no real-world evaluations about the effectiveness of such approaches in reducing energy consumption and about their impact on the end users.
In this paper, we present an A/B testing of four different fixed threshold-based carrier switch-off methods deployed in production networks serving large geographical regions.
Our study suggests that the capability of such strategies of reducing the energy costs hits a clear barrier if the end users' throughput must be preserved, and provides a strong empirical basis in support of more flexible approaches to save energy at the RAN.
%
%However, special attention and planning are needed to avoid reducing the user quality of experience, such as a lack of service or a significant drop in metrics like throughput. This work focuses on the impact of four different energy-saving approaches deployed on a live network in Europe and how they impact the network's performance and the users' Quality of Service.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Evaluation metrics}
\js{Move this to Sec 4??}

A main aspect behind optimizing energy saving in the RAN is evaluating the tradeoff between the energy saved and the impact on the users' performance\cite{Tan2022}. Thus, we take as a reference the following metrics as a proxy to monitor this tradeoff across the different policies and regions tested in the trials: 

\textbf{Total Downtime:} It measures the portion of PRBs utilized across all LTE cells in the regions. It serves as a proxy of the 

\textbf{Portion of cells affected:} It measures the portion of capacity cells where the energy saving policy applied at least 1\% of the time over the 1-week trial period.

\textbf{Overall Physical Resource Block Utilization:} It measures the portion of PRBs utilized across all LTE cells in the tested region. We use it as a proxy of the network congestion in that area.

\textbf{User average throughput:} \js{or delta throughput?}

\section{Energy saving policies in action}

As a first step we measure the percentage of downtime that the capacity booster experience during each week of trials. Fig~\ref{fig:percentage_downtime_capacity} show the results for each region. The policy \textit{24h (10/15)} switch off the carries for around 40\% of the time, that represent 67 carrier/hours. Interestingly the \textit{baseline} perform  relative similar to the \textit{24h (5/10)} policy.
In order to explore the reason behaving this metric, we explore how many capacity boosters meet the thresholds condition, show in Fig.~\ref{fig:fraction_antennas_affected}, and the percentage of time that this downtime of this fraction of antennas. Although the trials target around $44\%-47\%$ of the antennas in the regions, not all the antennas meet the switch-off thresholds.

A different view of the dynamic is showed on Fig.~\ref{fig:avail_policies_week} where it represent the mean average availability of the capacity boosters. As can be see, each policy presents a different behaviour.


In this section, we  take as a reference the week of Feb 8 to Feb 15, where there was a less dynamic energy saving policy (hereafter, \textit{Baseline}) deployed by the MNO at the country level. 

we define some sets to study the impact: I) the full TAC, ii) the set of antennas targeted by the policy that actually was affected, iii) the set of antennas targeted by the policy that was NOT affected, and iv) the set of antennas receiving the demand after the antennas switch off.

\section{Discussion \& Conclusion}

    \item o	The need for more aggressive/data-driven policies
